discovery: Optical detection and coherent control of individual electron and nuclear spins in solid-state defects (nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond), establishing solid-state spin qubits for quantum sensing and networking
subfield: Quantum physics / solid-state quantum information and sensing
motivation: Wrachtrup and Jelezko first optically detected magnetic resonance of a single defect spin in diamond, then demonstrated coherent control of single electron spins and their coupling to individual nuclear spins at room temperature. That turned an atom-like defect in a solid into a qubit that could be read out, controlled and engineered. Lukin's theoretical and experimental work showed how these spins could serve as nanoscale magnetometers, as long-lived nuclear-spin quantum memories and as nodes of quantum networks. Together their work founded a field. NV magnetometry now images neuronal currents, magnetic textures in condensed matter and paleomagnetism at nanometre resolution. Spin-photon entanglement between distant defects led to loophole-free Bell tests and multinode quantum networks. The same concepts drove the search for new hosts, from silicon carbide to rare-earth ions and molecules. This is a rare case where fundamental single-spin physics produced a new, broadly adopted measurement technology.
